newsitem.title: PERU: Search resumes at dawn for bodies in Peru mudslide.
newsitem.headline: Search resumes at dawn for bodies in Peru mudslide.

text.p: Rescuers prepared to resume their search at dawn on Wednesday for more than 100 people missing in the Peruvian Andes where a mountainside collapsed and a wall of mud swept away two villages, killing at least 33 people.
"Rescue brigades will go out in the morning and resume the search for bodies," said Julio Ocampo, assistant mayor of Abancay, capital of the stricken region in southeast Peru.
Mayor Luis Barra Pacheco said 33 bodies had been recovered from the mudslide which struck before dawn on Tuesday.

"Under the mud there are at least 100 people," he told Reuters, after darkness, heavy fog and further small landslides in the area prompted rescuers to call off the search for more victims at about 5 p.m. (2200 GMT) Tuesday.

The mayor said two other nearby villages, Kerapata and San Jorge, had also been evacuated because of the risk of mudslides and Abancay itself had been declared in a state of emergency because of snowfields in high mountains above the city.
"The snowfield has been cracking and if that continues we have to assume there could be further mudslides that would affect the city of Abancay directly," said Barra Pacheco.

Civil Defence workers, police, firefighters and Peruvian army units returning from the scene in Apurimac department, 380 miles (480 kms) southeast of Lima, said they had pulled dozens of bodies from the mud and seen many corpses mutilated by the rocks swept along in the torrents of mud.
"There were arms, heads, pieces of bodies sticking out of the mud," said firefighter. "We have tried to dig up the bodies using picks and shovels, but it's been difficult."
The mudslide occurred at about 4 a.m. (0900 GMT) Tuesday, virtually burying the villages of Ccocha and Pumaranra, near Abancay, which were home to nearly 250 people.
"Two villages have totally disappeared," said Barra Pacheco, estimating that 10.5 million cubic feet (300,000 cubic metres) of mud had slammed into the villages.

Police said the villages had been evacuated prior to the mudslide because of flooding over the weekend. But their refuge in a fold of the mountain just above the villages put them right in the path of the torrent of mud and boulders.
Civil Defence said it was sending 18 tons of supplies to the region for survivors, as well as three dogs to help find bodies and a geologist to assess further risks.

Police said reports from villagers indicated 50 to 60 families were buried. The mayor's office faxed a list to Reuters with the names of 134 villagers reported missing, among them entire families. But Abancay officials said the number of casualties was probably closer to between 150 and 200.

Rescue workers prepared to evacuate more than 60 families Wednesday from towns near the disaster zone to schools on the outskirts of Abancay, in case of further slides. Ccocha and Pumaranra are about six miles (10 kms) east of Abancay.
Alejandro Caballero, mayor of the neighbouring village of Tamburco, said he believed there were more than 200 people missing. "No one has survived there," he said.
Flash floods, mudslides and landslides are common in Peru's Andes during the January-March rainy season.
Over the weekend, five people died in flooding in Tamburco and floods in the jungle province of Rioja destroyed the homes of 500 families and swept away a woman and two children.
